claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure.
The hierarchical heterostructure remains intact after the stated standard processing conditions.
High-resolution imaging can provide quantitative descriptors of grain or subgrain boundaries and phase distributions in HfNbTiVAl10.
A machine-learning surrogate can be calibrated using these microstructural descriptors and tensile and fracture test data.
Grain boundaries, phase distributions, and multiscale defect structures govern the mechanical response of the hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 heterostructure.
Statistically significant correlations exist between well-resolved microstructural features and tensile and fracture responses.
Direct incorporation of microstructural descriptors will make the ML model more accurate than established physics-based simulations lacking those details.
The ML surrogate bypasses iterative, computation-intensive steps used by conventional simulations.
By bypassing those simulation steps, the ML surrogate will reduce prediction time.
The ML surrogate will predict Young's modulus in HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately than the baseline simulations.
The ML surrogate will predict yield strength in HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately than the baseline simulations.
The ML surrogate will predict fracture toughness in HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately than the baseline simulations.
The ML surrogate will require significantly less computational prediction time than conventional simulation methods.
Failure to capture critical microstructural features may prevent the proposed accuracy improvement.
Evolution of the heterostructure during testing that is absent from the training data may degrade model performance.
Extrapolation beyond the calibration regime may reduce the effectiveness of the ML model.
The direction of improvement in predictive accuracy and efficiency is supported.
The magnitude of gains in accuracy and efficiency cannot be established until calibration and statistical validation are completed.
